title: How do you compare two values safely when either may be null?
shortTitle: How do you compare two values safely when either may be null?
keyPoints: Objects.equals(a, b): null-safe, returns true if both null, false if one is null
"constant".equals(variable): null-safe because the constant is never null
Optional.ofNullable(x).orElse(default): convert null to a default value before comparing
Avoid a.equals(b) when a might be null – throws NullPointerException
Understanding this concept is essential for Java interviews at senior level

s1_definition.oneliner: Use Objects.equals(a, b) for null-safe comparison. It handles null on both sides without throwing NullPointerException.
s1_definition.profdef:
Three null-safe comparison techniques:

- **Objects.equals(a, b):** Handles all cases. `null, null → true`. `null, non-null → false`. `non-null, non-null → a.equals(b)`.
- **"literal".equals(variable):** Put the known non-null value on the left.
- **Optional:** `Optional.ofNullable(x).map(...).orElse(false)` for complex comparisons.
s1_definition.analogy: When comparing two bank forms, always check if either form is missing (null) before reading its contents. Objects.equals is the clerk who handles missing forms gracefully instead of crashing.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  a.equals(b)           → NPE if a is null
  Objects.equals(a, b)  → safe: handles null on both sides
  "literal".equals(var)  → safe: literal is never null
  Optional.ofNullable(x).orElse(default) → convert null first
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Use Objects.equals(a, b) for null-safe comparison. It handles all null combinations without throwing NPE. In equals() implementations, use Objects.equals for each field comparison.

One sentence to remember: Objects.equals(a, b) is null-safe – use it instead of a.equals(b) when either side might be null.
